AD 70: Jerusalem and the temple destroyed

Roman forces under Titus captured Jerusalem in AD 70 after a long siege and burned the second temple. Josephus describes great loss of life and the taking of many captives. Jesus had foretold this judgment in Luke 19:41-44 and Luke 21:20-24. Jewish life continued in Galilee and in the wider diaspora, but the temple and its sacrifices ended.
AD 132-135: Bar Kokhba revolt and Aelia Capitolina

A second Jewish revolt, led by Simon bar Kosiba (called Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star'), was crushed by Hadrian's armies by AD 135. Rabbi Akiva is reported to have hailed Bar Kokhba as the Messiah. Hadrian refounded Jerusalem as a Roman colony, Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were barred from entering the city. The province was renamed Syria Palaestina; whether this was meant as a punishment is disputed among historians.
1609: Thomas Brightman and the Puritan hope

The English Puritan Thomas Brightman (1562-1607) argued in his commentary on Revelation, Apocalypsis Apocalypseos (published 1609), that the Jews would be converted to Christ and return to their land. This joined two ideas that many later Puritans held together: a future large-scale conversion of the Jews (from Romans 11:25-26) and a future return to the land. Brightman expected the conversion first; for him, return followed faith.
1655-56: Jews readmitted to England

The Amsterdam rabbi Menasseh ben Israel petitioned Oliver Cromwell to readmit Jews to England, from which they had been expelled in 1290. The Whitehall Conference of December 1655 reached no formal decision, but Jewish residence was tolerated from 1656. Puritan hopes for the conversion of the Jews formed part of the background, alongside trade and religious toleration.
1669: Increase Mather, The Mystery of Israel's Salvation

The New England minister Increase Mather (1639-1723) published The Mystery of Israel's Salvation Explained and Applyed (London, 1669). He argued that the Jewish people would be converted in large numbers and restored to their land before the end. Like most restorationists of this era, he tied the return to conversion, not to a political project. Iain Murray's The Puritan Hope traces this tradition.
1831-33: J. N. Darby and the Powerscourt conferences

John Nelson Darby (1800-1882), a leader of the Plymouth Brethren, developed his teaching at prophecy meetings such as the Powerscourt conferences in Ireland (1831-1833). He drew a sharp line between Israel (God's earthly people) and the church (God's heavenly people) and taught a secret rapture of the church before God resumes His dealings with Israel. This system, later called dispensationalism, gave restoration a new shape: Israel could return to the land in unbelief before its national conversion.
1838-1840s: Lord Shaftesbury and restorationism in Britain

Anthony Ashley-Cooper, later the seventh Earl of Shaftesbury, an evangelical, urged the British government to support Jewish return to Palestine. Britain opened a vice-consulate in Jerusalem in 1838, and in 1840 Shaftesbury pressed Foreign Secretary Palmerston to sponsor Jewish settlement. The slogan 'a land without a people for a people without a land' is often credited to him. Its attribution is contested: similar wording appears in the Scottish minister Alexander Keith (1843) and in Shaftesbury's later writings, and Israel Zangwill popularised it around 1901. The phrase is also disputed in substance, since the land had a settled Arab population.
1881-82: Russian pogroms and the First Aliyah

After the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in March 1881, waves of anti-Jewish riots (pogroms) swept the south-western Russian Empire. The restrictive 'May Laws' of 1882 followed. Most Jews who left went to the United States, but small groups such as Bilu and Hovevei Zion (Lovers of Zion) began the First Aliyah (1882-1903), founding farming settlements such as Rishon LeZion (1882). Their motive was mainly safety and national renewal, not the fulfilment of prophecy.
1891: The Blackstone Memorial

William E. Blackstone, a Chicago businessman and author of the premillennial bestseller Jesus Is Coming (1878), presented a petition to President Benjamin Harrison in March 1891. It asked the United States to support giving Palestine back to the Jews and was signed by over 400 prominent Americans, including business leaders, editors and clergy. No action followed, but the Memorial is often cited as an early landmark of American Christian Zionism.
1896: Theodor Herzl, Der Judenstaat

The Viennese journalist Theodor Herzl (1860-1904) published Der Judenstaat ('The Jewish State') in February 1896. He argued that antisemitism would not disappear in Europe and that Jews needed a state of their own, secured by international agreement. His case was political and largely secular; he even considered places other than Palestine. The Dreyfus affair in France (from 1894) is often linked to his thinking, though how much it shaped him is disputed.
1897: First Zionist Congress, Basel

Herzl convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel, Switzerland, on 29-31 August 1897. It founded the Zionist Organization and adopted the Basel Program, which aimed to create for the Jewish people a home in Palestine 'secured by public law'. Most delegates were secular or traditional rather than strictly Orthodox, and many leading Orthodox rabbis opposed the movement at this time.
1909: The Scofield Reference Bible

Oxford University Press published the Scofield Reference Bible, edited by C. I. Scofield, in 1909 (revised 1917). Its notes spread Darby's dispensational scheme, including a future national restoration of Israel, among millions of English-speaking Protestants. Many readers met the Israel-church distinction in the margin of their Bibles rather than in theology books.
1917: The Balfour Declaration

On 2 November 1917, Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour wrote to Lord Rothschild that the British government viewed with favour 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine. The same letter said nothing should be done to prejudice the civil and religious rights of the existing non-Jewish communities. British motives included wartime strategy, imperial interests near the Suez Canal, and the hope of Jewish support for the Allies; some cabinet members also held restorationist sympathies. In December 1917 General Allenby's forces entered Jerusalem, ending Ottoman rule there.
1920-22: The British Mandate for Palestine

The San Remo conference (April 1920) assigned Palestine to Britain, and the League of Nations approved the Mandate in July 1922; it took effect in 1923. The Mandate text included the Balfour Declaration's commitment to a Jewish national home. In the same period Britain separated Transjordan from the area open to Jewish settlement. Jewish immigration and land purchase grew, and so did Arab opposition, with serious violence in 1920, 1921 and 1929.
1933-45: The Holocaust

From the Nazi seizure of power in 1933, Jews in Germany faced growing persecution, and during the Second World War some six million Jews were murdered in a deliberate programme of genocide. Many survivors had no homes to return to, and many were held in displaced persons camps after 1945. The Holocaust convinced much of the world, and most Jews, that a Jewish state was a necessity for safety.
1937: The Peel Commission proposes partition

After the Arab revolt began in 1936, a British Royal Commission led by Lord Peel reported in July 1937 that the Mandate was unworkable. It proposed dividing the land into a small Jewish state and an Arab state joined to Transjordan, with a British zone around Jerusalem. The Zionist leadership was divided but open to negotiation; the Arab Higher Committee rejected it. The plan was later dropped.
1939: The British White Paper

In May 1939 the British government issued a White Paper limiting Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years, restricting land sales, and proposing an independent Palestine within ten years. It aimed to secure Arab goodwill as war with Germany approached. Zionists saw it as a betrayal, coming just as European Jews most needed refuge.
1947: UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181)

On 29 November 1947 the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 181 by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions. It recommended ending the Mandate and dividing the land into a Jewish state and an Arab state, with Jerusalem under an international regime. The Jewish Agency accepted the plan; the Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected it. Fighting between Jewish and Arab communities broke out almost at once.
14 May 1948: The State of Israel is declared

On 14 May 1948, the day before the Mandate ended, David Ben-Gurion read the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel in Tel Aviv. The text grounds the state in Jewish history, the Balfour Declaration, the Holocaust and the UN resolution. It speaks of trust in the 'Rock of Israel', a phrase chosen so that both religious and secular signers could accept it. The United States recognised the state within minutes (de facto), and the Soviet Union gave full legal recognition three days later.
1948-49: The war and Palestinian displacement

Armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered the conflict on 15 May 1948. By the 1949 armistice agreements Israel held more territory than the partition plan had assigned; Egypt held Gaza and Transjordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem. About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from their homes and were not allowed to return; Palestinians call this the Nakba ('catastrophe'). The causes and the balance of flight and expulsion are debated by historians. In the following decades a comparable number of Jews left or were driven from Arab and Muslim countries, many settling in Israel.
1950: The Law of Return

On 5 July 1950 Israel's parliament (the Knesset) passed the Law of Return, giving every Jew the right to settle in Israel as a citizen. A 1970 amendment extended this to children and grandchildren of Jews and their spouses. The law defines the state's purpose as a refuge for Jews; it is a civil law, not a religious decree, and the question 'who is a Jew' under it has been debated in Israel ever since.
1967: The Six-Day War and East Jerusalem

In the war of 5-10 June 1967, Israel took Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. Israeli troops reached the Western Wall on 7 June. Israel later applied its law to East Jerusalem; most states and the UN have not recognised this annexation. For many evangelical prophecy writers this event was decisive: L. Nelson Bell wrote in Christianity Today (July 1967) that Jerusalem being wholly in Jewish hands for the first time in over 2,000 years gave new confidence in the Bible, and Luke 21:24 became a central proof-text.
1970: Hal Lindsey, The Late Great Planet Earth

Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (Zondervan, 1970), written with C. C. Carlson, became one of the best-selling non-fiction books in the United States in the 1970s. It read 1948 as the budding of the fig tree (Matthew 24:32-34) and suggested that the end-time events would come within about forty years, one generation, of 1948. It also identified Russia with Gog of Ezekiel 38. The book brought dispensational prophecy about Israel into popular culture.
1973: The Yom Kippur War

On 6 October 1973, the Day of Atonement, Egypt and Syria attacked Israeli positions in Sinai and the Golan Heights. After heavy losses and early setbacks, Israel regained the initiative; a ceasefire came later that month. Arab oil producers imposed an oil embargo on states that backed Israel. Prophecy writing responded quickly, for example John Walvoord's Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis (1974).
1980: International Christian Embassy Jerusalem

In 1980 Israel's Knesset passed the Jerusalem Law, and the UN Security Council (Resolution 478) called on states to withdraw their embassies from the city; thirteen states moved their embassies to Tel Aviv. In September 1980 a group of Christians founded the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (ICEJ) as an expression of Christian support for Israel. It became a major voice of global Christian Zionism, known for its annual Feast of Tabernacles gathering.
1988: '88 Reasons' and failed date-setting

Edgar C. Whisenant, a retired NASA engineer, published 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988, distributing millions of copies. He set the rapture at Rosh Hashanah, 11-13 September 1988, partly on the reasoning that 1948 plus a forty-year generation gave 1988. The date passed, as did his later revised dates. Earlier, Chuck Smith's Future Survival (1978) had suggested the rapture might come by 1981. These failures led many dispensationalists to warn against fixing dates from 1948.
2006: Christians United for Israel

Pastor John Hagee of Cornerstone Church, San Antonio, founded Christians United for Israel (CUFI) in February 2006. It grew into one of the largest pro-Israel organisations in the United States and lobbies on US policy. Its leaders often cite Genesis 12:3 as the biblical basis for supporting the State of Israel.
2017-18: The US embassy moves to Jerusalem

On 6 December 2017 the United States formally recognised Jerusalem as Israel's capital, and on 14 May 2018 it opened its embassy there. Many evangelical leaders welcomed the move and some described it in prophetic terms; many other states and church bodies criticised it. The final status of Jerusalem remains a matter of international dispute.
The secular nationalist character of early Zionism

Political Zionism was led mainly by secular or non-observant Jews. Theodor Herzl's Der Judenstaat (1896) argued from the failure of emancipation and the persistence of antisemitism, not from prophecy, and Herzl was willing in 1903 to consider a British offer of land in East Africa (the 'Uganda scheme'). Labour Zionists such as David Ben-Gurion built the state's institutions on socialist and national ideals. The movement drew on the ancient Jewish bond with the land, but its programme was a modern national one, similar to other European nationalisms of the time.
European antisemitism and the pogroms

The Russian pogroms of 1881-82 and 1903-06 (including Kishinev, 1903), the May Laws, and the Dreyfus affair in France convinced many Jews that legal equality in Europe would not protect them. This pushed emigration, mostly to America, and gave Zionism its urgent case. The movement was therefore in large part a response to persecution, much of it in historically Christian lands.
British imperial strategy

Britain issued the Balfour Declaration (1917) during the First World War for several reasons: to protect the approaches to the Suez Canal and India, to secure a post-war foothold in Palestine against French claims, and to win Jewish support in Russia and America for the Allies. Some leaders, such as Lloyd George and Balfour, also had restorationist sympathies from their Bible-reading upbringing. Britain then governed the land under a League of Nations Mandate (1922-1948), and its shifting policies, from the Balfour promise to the 1939 White Paper, shaped events decisively.
The Holocaust and world sympathy

The murder of some six million Jews in 1933-45, and the plight of about a quarter of a million Jewish displaced persons after the war, gave the Zionist case moral force in world opinion. Western states, including the United States, had largely closed their doors to Jewish refugees before and during the war. Many delegates at the United Nations in 1947 were moved by the need for a Jewish refuge.
The UN vote and superpower recognition

The UN General Assembly's partition resolution (Resolution 181, 29 November 1947) gave international legitimacy to a Jewish state, and both the United States and the Soviet Union voted for it. President Truman recognised Israel within minutes of its declaration on 14 May 1948, against the advice of some of his State Department officials; the USSR followed with full recognition on 17 May. Soviet-bloc arms (notably from Czechoslovakia) reached Jewish forces in 1948. The founding thus depended on Cold War diplomacy as well as on events on the ground.
The military outcome of the 1948-49 war

The state's borders were set not by the partition map but by the fighting of 1947-49 and the 1949 armistice lines. Jewish forces, better organised and later better armed, defeated Palestinian militias and then the invading Arab armies. During the war about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled, and Israel did not permit their return; Palestinians call this the Nakba. Historians still debate the causes, but they agree the outcome was decided by military and political means.
Religious Zionism's later role

A minority of Orthodox Jews supported Zionism from the start. Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook (1865-1935), Chief Rabbi in Mandate Palestine, taught that secular pioneers were unknowingly serving God's redemptive plan. Religious Zionism grew much stronger after 1967, when the capture of the Old City and the West Bank was read by some as 'the beginning of redemption'. But in 1948 the state's founders were mostly secular, and many Haredi (strictly Orthodox) Jews opposed a Jewish state before the Messiah.
Christian Zionist lobbying

Protestant restorationism, from the Puritans to Lord Shaftesbury and William Blackstone's 1891 Memorial, helped create a climate in Britain and America that was friendly to Jewish return. Historians differ on how much it affected actual decisions in 1917 and 1948; most see it as one factor among many, more cultural than decisive. Its political influence grew mainly after 1967, through organisations such as the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (1980) and Christians United for Israel (2006).
Isaiah asks whether a land can be born in one day or a nation brought forth at once. The claim is that this was fulfilled on 14 May 1948, when Israel was declared a state in a single day.
Widely used in popular prophecy preaching and Christian Zionist writing, for example by John Hagee, and repeated in much evangelical media each year around Israel's independence day.

The verse speaks of a nation coming into being suddenly, and on 14 May 1948 a Jewish state did appear in one day after nearly 1,900 years without one. The context (Isaiah 66:7-9) speaks of Zion giving birth before labour pains, which proponents link to the speed of the declaration. They see the match between the words and the event as too striking to be chance.

The fulfilment reading notes that Isaiah 66 is about Zion's children after judgment, with mother-and-birth imagery for a restored people (Isaiah 66:10-13), not a modern political declaration. The birth comes before the pain (66:7), whereas 1948 came after the Holocaust and amid war. Isaiah 66:18-23 goes on to the gathering of all nations and the new heavens and new earth, which the New Testament applies to the age of the gospel and its consummation (compare Galatians 4:26-27, where Paul quotes Isaiah 54:1 about the barren mother and applies it to the Jerusalem above). Critics also note that the process of founding a state took decades, from 1897 to 1949, so 'in one day' fits only the act of declaring it.

Proponents answer that prophecy often has a near and a far fulfilment, and that the sudden legal birth of a state is a fair reading of 'at once'. They argue that the striking parallel is meant to draw attention, and that Isaiah 66:20 still speaks of Israel's people being brought from all nations to Jerusalem.
A striking parallel in wording; whether it is a prediction of 1948 depends on how one reads the whole chapter, and the New Testament does not use it this way.
Ezekiel's vision of dry bones that come together, gain flesh, and only then receive breath is read as a picture of Israel's return to the land in unbelief (1948) followed later by spiritual rebirth.
Classic dispensationalists such as John Walvoord and J. Dwight Pentecost, Messianic Jewish writer Arnold Fruchtenbaum, and popular writers such as Hal Lindsey.

God explains the vision: the bones are 'the whole house of Israel', and He will open their graves and bring them into the land of Israel (Ezekiel 37:11-12). The vision has two stages: the bones join and gain flesh but have no breath (37:7-8), then the breath enters (37:9-10). Proponents read 1948 as the first stage, a physical regathering in unbelief, with the second stage, national faith in the Messiah, still to come (compare Zechariah 12:10). Ezekiel 37:15-28 then promises one nation under one king, David, which they read as a future reunited Israel under Christ.

Fulfilment scholars note that the vision addresses exiles who say 'our hope is lost' (37:11) in the sixth century BC, and was first fulfilled in the return from Babylon under Cyrus (Ezra 1:1-4). The breath is God's Spirit (37:14), and the New Testament links the giving of the Spirit and new life to Christ's resurrection and Pentecost (John 20:22; Acts 2:33). The 'David' who reigns (37:24-25) is the risen Christ, now enthroned (Acts 2:30-36). Critics add that the conditions of return in the Law (Deuteronomy 30:1-3) put turning to the LORD first, and that a two-stage modern reading puts more weight on verse 8 than the text gives it.

Dispensationalists answer that the order in Ezekiel 37 is explicit: gathering of bodies first, then breath. They argue that the Babylonian return did not unite Israel and Judah under David for ever (37:22-25) or bring a permanent covenant of peace and God's sanctuary among them for evermore (37:26-28), so a further fulfilment is required. On their view, Deuteronomy 30 describes the final, complete restoration, while partial returns can precede it.
The strongest text for a return before faith; the debate turns on whether the Babylonian return and the Spirit-giving in Christ exhaust it.

Jesus' parable of the fig tree putting out leaves is taken to mean Israel's rebirth in 1948, and 'this generation will not pass away' to mean that the generation that saw 1948 would see Christ's return.
Hal Lindsey (The Late Great Planet Earth, 1970), who suggested the end-time events would come within about forty years of 1948; Chuck Smith (Future Survival, 1978); Edgar Whisenant (1988).

The fig tree is used elsewhere as a symbol of Israel (Jeremiah 24:1-10; Hosea 9:10; Luke 13:6-9), and Jesus cursed a fruitless fig tree (Matthew 21:18-20). Proponents argued that the tree putting out leaves again is the nation's revival, and 'this generation' is the generation that sees these signs. Read this way, 1948 starts a countdown.

Critics note that in the parallel passage Jesus says 'the fig tree, and all the trees' (Luke 21:29), so the point is a general lesson from nature: when you see the signs, the event is near. In Matthew, 'this generation' elsewhere means Jesus' own hearers (Matthew 23:36), and the signs he lists were fulfilled in the destruction of the temple in AD 70 (Matthew 24:1-2, 15-21). Most strikingly, the forty-year reading failed: 1988 and its variants passed without the predicted events. Many dispensational scholars themselves rejected the 1948 reading of the fig tree.

Many dispensational scholars, such as Thomas Ice, agree that the 1948 date-setting was a mistake and that the fig tree is not a symbol of Israel here. They read 'this generation' as the generation alive when the end-time signs begin, which is still future, so the passage is not tied to 1948. Lindsey himself later qualified his forty-year suggestion.
The clearest example of a failed prophetic timeline built on 1948; the text is now read in other ways even by most futurist scholars.

Jeremiah says a day will come when people will no longer swear by the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt, but by the LORD who brought them from the land of the north and from all lands. This is read as the modern return, especially of Jews from Russia and the former Soviet Union.

Popular Christian Zionist writers and ministries that fund Jewish immigration, such as Derek Prince (The Last Word on the Middle East, 1982) and organisations that help Jews from the former Soviet Union settle in Israel; also Arnold Fruchtenbaum.

The text promises a return so great that it will eclipse the exodus from Egypt as Israel's defining memory. Proponents note that over a million Jews emigrated from the Soviet Union and its successor states to Israel, mostly after 1989, which fits 'the land of the north'. They also stress 'all lands' (16:15) as wider than Babylon alone, and the promise to bring them into 'their land which I gave to their fathers'.

Fulfilment scholars read 'the land of the north' as Babylon, which in Jeremiah is consistently the enemy from the north (Jeremiah 1:13-15; 6:22; 25:9). The promise was given to people facing the Babylonian exile and was fulfilled in the return from 539 BC onwards. The surrounding verses (16:19-21) look to the nations turning to the LORD, which the New Testament sees in the gospel. Critics add that a return mainly by secular migration does not match Jeremiah's linking of restoration with repentance (Jeremiah 29:12-14).

Proponents answer that the return from Babylon did not overshadow the exodus in Israel's memory, as the text predicts, and was not from 'all lands'. They hold that only a worldwide return, such as the one since 1882, matches the scale, and that the passage says nothing about faith coming before return.
Plausible as an extended application, but the text's own setting points first to Babylon; the size of the modern return is a fact both sides must weigh.

God promises to plant Israel in their land so that they will never again be pulled up out of it. Since Israel was uprooted after the Babylonian return (in AD 70 and 135), proponents argue this must refer to the modern return, which will be permanent.
Walter Kaiser, John Walvoord, Arnold Fruchtenbaum and many Christian Zionists.

Amos promises restored fortunes, rebuilt cities, vineyards and gardens, and a planting that will never be uprooted (9:14-15). After the return from Babylon, Jerusalem was again destroyed in AD 70, so, the argument goes, the 'never again' was not yet fulfilled. Proponents conclude that the final, permanent planting is either 1948 or still future. Walter Kaiser argued that Acts 15 confirms the Gentile part of Amos 9 without cancelling the national part.

Fulfilment scholars point out that James quotes the first part of this passage, the rebuilding of David's fallen tent (Amos 9:11-12), as fulfilled in the inclusion of the Gentiles through Christ (Acts 15:14-18). If the restored house of David is the risen Christ and his people, the land-planting that follows belongs to the same restoration, and its final form is the renewed earth (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5). The Law tied secure dwelling to covenant faithfulness (Leviticus 26:3-5, 33; Deuteronomy 30:1-3). Critics add that a secular state's continuing existence since 1948 cannot by itself prove that 'never again' applies to it.

Dispensationalists answer that Acts 15 cites Amos to show that Gentile inclusion agrees with the prophets, not to say that Amos is exhausted. They argue the plain sense of 'never be uprooted from the land I have given them' is a physical land, and that the church cannot be 'planted' in Canaan. Many do not claim 1948 is the final planting; they expect it after Israel's national repentance.
A real promise of permanent planting; the question is whether Acts 15 shows its fulfilment in Christ and the new creation or leaves a national land phase still to come.

Isaiah says the Lord will set His hand 'the second time' to recover the remnant of His people from many lands. Proponents count the return from Babylon as the first time and the modern return as the second.
John Walvoord, Arnold Fruchtenbaum, Hal Lindsey and many popular writers.

The verse lists distant places (Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath and the coastlands) and says the gathering will be from 'the four corners of the earth' (11:12). Proponents argue that the return from Babylon was the first regathering, so a second worldwide one must be later. They see the modern return from over a hundred countries as matching this scope.

Critics note that the context counts the exodus from Egypt as the first act of redemption: verse 16 compares this gathering with the day Israel came up out of Egypt. So the 'second time' would naturally be the return from exile, Assyria and Babylon included. Paul quotes the previous verse, about the root of Jesse whom the nations will seek (Isaiah 11:10), as fulfilled in the Gentiles' faith in Christ (Romans 15:12). That places the whole passage in the messianic age begun by Christ.

Proponents answer that the return from Babylon was not from Cush, Elam and the coastlands, nor from 'the four corners of the earth', so the full scope of 11:11-12 points to a later worldwide gathering. They accept Romans 15:12 but hold that the Gentile blessing and the Jewish regathering both belong to the messianic age, whose national side is still to come.
Turns on how 'second' is counted; the exodus comparison in verse 16 favours the exile reading, while the wide geography gives the futurist reading some weight.

God says He will take Israel from the nations and bring them into their own land, and then sprinkle clean water on them and give them a new heart. Proponents see the order as gathering first (1948) and cleansing later.
Arnold Fruchtenbaum, John Walvoord, Michael Vlach and many Christian Zionists.

The sequence in the text is gathering into the land (36:24), then cleansing (36:25), then the new heart and the Spirit (36:26-27), then dwelling in the land given to the fathers (36:28). Proponents argue this shows a return in unbelief followed by spiritual renewal, matching the modern situation in which most Israelis are not believers in Jesus. They add that God acts 'not for your sake' but for His holy name (36:22), so the return does not depend on Israel's merit.

Fulfilment scholars note that the passage is the new covenant promise, and Jesus alludes to it when He speaks of being born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5; compare Ezekiel 36:25-27). The New Testament presents the new heart and the Spirit as given now to Jews and Gentiles in Christ (2 Corinthians 3:3; Hebrews 8:8-12). Hebrew narrative and prophecy often list connected acts without strict order, so the verse order does not prove a time gap. Critics also cite Deuteronomy 30:1-3, where return follows repentance.
